sections.history: Pavana Narasimha is the most secluded of the nine Narasimha shrines of Ahobilam, set on the bank of the Pavana stream, from which it takes its name. It lies some six to seven kilometres from Upper Ahobilam by forest footpath, or considerably farther by a rough jeep track through the Nallamala forest from Lower Ahobilam. Its remoteness has kept it close to the Chenchu, the forest-dwelling people of these hills, whose bond with Narasimha runs through Ahobilam's traditions. The shrine is within the Ahobila Matha's worship of the nine forms, and pilgrims regard reaching it as the crowning effort of the Nava Narasimha yatra.
sections.architecture: The temple is a small shrine in a forest clearing by the stream, with a simple mandapa before the sanctum. Here Narasimha is seated with Lakshmi, revered locally as Chenchu Lakshmi, at his side, and a separate shrine to Chenchu Lakshmi stands nearby. The setting — dense forest, running water and hills on every side — is as much a part of the darshan as the stone.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that the sage Bharadwaja performed penance here and was freed from a grave sin through the grace of Narasimha; pavana means purifying, and the place is held to cleanse all who come with devotion. Chenchu tradition holds that Lakshmi was born among them as Chenchu Lakshmi and wed the Lord after he had slain Hiranyakashipu. In the astrological reading of the nine shrines, Pavana is linked with Mercury.
sections.festivals: Narasimha Jayanti and the annual Brahmotsavam of Ahobilam are the main occasions; weekends and festival days bring a stream of jeeps along the forest track. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: This is a journey for the prepared. The jeep ride is long and jolting and fords streams; the walking route from Upper Ahobilam is a full forest trek. Forest officials control entry and turn vehicles back late in the day, so set out in the morning. Carry water and food — there are few facilities in the forest.

visit.timings: Worship is offered daily, but forest access is regulated by the Forest Department and vehicles are not allowed in late in the day; set out in the morning. Confirm current timings and access rules locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: From Lower Ahobilam (reached by road via Allagadda; Nandyal is the nearest major railhead), hire a local four-wheel-drive jeep for the forest track; private vehicles are generally not permitted. A footpath of about six to seven kilometres also leads from Upper Ahobilam; go with a local guide.
